subject: chemistry
question_text: Define the following terms: a) Entropy b) Heat capacity c) Absolute entropy

verification.note: Unit 6 Thermodynamics is sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack chemistry section (book pp.73-75), which prints the question, its star rank and a model answer. Only ONE source book is held for chemistry — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only — so the two-book union check is PENDING a second chemistry source. This chapter has NO Long Answer section in the book, so no 8-mark form is invented. The 1+1 mark split over three definitions is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Entropy and heat capacity
lines: a) Entropy (S): a measure of the randomness
or disorder of a system. It is a state
b) Heat capacity (C): the amount of heat
required to raise the temperature of a
steps.why: Both are definitions the examiner checks word by word: entropy needs disorder of a system, and heat capacity needs one degree.
common_mistakes: Defining heat capacity per gram — that is specific heat capacity.
Writing that entropy is a form of energy. It is a measure of disorder, with units J K⁻¹.
steps.memory_tip: S for scatter: the more scattered the particles, the higher the entropy. C answers one question: how much heat for one degree?
steps.margin_note: Two short definitions; one or two lines each is enough.

steps.label: Absolute entropy
lines: c) Absolute entropy: the entropy of one mole
of a pure substance in its standard state
It is counted from the true zero fixed by
the third law: S = 0 at 0 K.

lines.text: Absolute entropy: entropy of one mole at 298 K, standard state

steps.why: The third law fixes S = 0 for a perfect crystal at 0 K, so a real total (absolute) entropy can be counted from that zero. The source book prints the standard state as 273 K; standard thermodynamic data are reported at 298 K, so this card writes 298 K.
common_mistakes: Writing 273 K for the standard state — thermodynamic tables use 298 K.
steps.memory_tip: Absolute means counted from a true zero: S = 0 at 0 K for a perfect crystal.
steps.margin_note: 298 K and one mole are the two details to include.

insider_note: Three definitions share two marks, so each must be one tight line — long answers here cost time, not marks.
